text:
Droit de la famille -- 21910

2021 QCCS 2081

SUPERIOR COURT

(Family Division)

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-12-344308-196

DATE:

20 MAY 2021

_____________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

BABAK BARIN, J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________

J. B.

Plaintiff

v.

A. M.

Defendant

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT ON transfer of
Proceedings,
FORUM NON CONVENIENS
& PARENTing TIME SHARE

ArTICLES 6 & 16 OF
THE
DIVORCE ACT

ARTICLES 3093, 3135 &
3142 C.C.Q.

_____________________________________________________________________

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

“X” as his name is pronounced in French is just over two years old.
He was born in City A with certain medical complications but has now
fortunately overcome them and is living, as permitted by an order of this Court,
with his mother close to the City B. X likes to read books and repeat words after
his parents in French, English, Greek and Arabic.

[
2
]

X’s father is of Greek origin and his mother is of Arabic decent.
His father, lives in City A and manages two revenue properties. He does not
hold a full-time employment preferring instead to be available to visit his son
in Ontario and spend time with him. He seeks equal parenting time with respect
to X.

[
3
]

X’s mother considers that equal parenting time is premature and is of
the view that, despite the fact that the divorce proceedings filed at her
behest are pending in this province, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice is
better suited to decide, at a minimum, all future parenting-related applications
in regards to X. She concedes, however, that the Quebec Superior Court is
provisionally competent to address the pending parenting time and other issues raised
by Monsieur.

[
4
]

The recent revisions to the
Divorce Act
[1]
, the majority of which came
into force on 1 March 2021, reflect the changes that were needed in family law in
the eyes of the Canadian Parliament to better serve the much evolved Canadian
society – this country is not the same as it was 36 years ago – and ensure that
children’s best interests are prioritized. The
Act
received Royal Assent
on 21 June 2019. The changes reflect the most extensive revisions in decades
and show credence to Canada’s growing multicultural society.

[
5
]

Among other things, the
Act
replaces the old language of
custody of and access to a child of the marriage with parenting time orders that
are to favour a more win-win rather than a winner-loser regime among married
parents. The
Act
also moves away from any notion of equal parenting time
presumption and emphasizes in line with
section 33
of the
Quebec
Civil Code

(
C.C.Q.
) that the best interests of an individual child must govern any
decision concerning him or her.

[
6
]

To that end, the
Act
includes expansive and non-exhaustive
factors that may be considered as a starting mark in defining a child’s best
interests. With respect to parenting orders specifically, the
Act
provides
that if an application for a parenting order is made in a divorce or corollary
relief proceeding to a court in a province and “the child of the marriage in
respect of whom the order is sought is habitually resident in another province,
the court
may
, on application by a spouse or on its own motion, transfer
the proceeding to a court in that other province.”
[2]

[
7
]

It is useful to recall that
section 6
of the
Act
removes the
requirement that the application be opposed. Habitual residence is a well-known
notion in international conventions to which Canada has adhered to and it must be
determined on a case by case basis and based on all circumstances.

[
8
]

The
Act
provides that either or both spouses, or a person,
other than a spouse, who is a parent of the child, standing in the place of a
parent or intending to stand in the place of a parent, may make an application
for parenting time or decision-making responsibility in respect of any child of
the marriage
[3]
.
Parenting time may be allocated by way of a schedule
[4]
.

[
9
]

The
Act
also specifies that if a court in a province is
seized of an application for a parenting order in respect of a child of the
marriage, the court has jurisdiction to hear and determine an application for a
contact order in respect of that child.”
[5]

A contact order with respect to a child of the marriage may be sought by a
person other than a spouse. A contact order is
not
a parenting order. The
granting of a contact order is not relevant in this case.

[
10
]

In making a parenting order, the
Act

explicitly
requires the court to
only
consider the best interests of the child.
While in determining such an interest the court is required to take into consideration
certain specified factors like the nature and strength of the child’s
relationship with each spouse, the married parents’ ability and willingness to care
for and meet the needs of the child and communicate and cooperate with one
another on matters affecting the child, on the child’s cultural, linguistic,
religious and spiritual upbringing and heritage, and the presence of any family
violence – the primary consideration remains the child’s physical, emotional
and psychological safety, security and well-being.
[6]

[
11
]

Moreover, in allocating parenting time, the
court must give effect to the principle that “a child should have as much
time

with each spouse – to use the conscious and concise words of the statute – as
is consistent with the best interests of the child.”
[7]
Prior to the amendments, the
statute used to require that courts give effect to the principle that a child
of a marriage should have as much
contact
with each spouse as was
consistent with the child’s best interests.

[
12
]

Finally, in evaluating the best interests of the
child, the court shall
not
take into consideration past conduct, “unless
the conduct is relevant to the exercise of […] parenting time, decision making
responsibility or contact with the child under a contact order.”
[8]

CONTEXT

[
13
]

X’s parents met online in 2014. At the time, his
mother was completing an MBA in City C and his father lived in City A. In 2016,
his parents decided to move to Ontario. Madame moved in June followed by
Monsieur in July. The parties were married in a religious ceremony in Greece on
20 August 2017. X was conceived in the early spring of 2018 with a due date in
December. His parents were married in a civil ceremony in City A on 23 August
2018. At the time, the parties opted to be married with a marriage contract
adopting the regime of separation as to property.

[
14
]

In July of 2018, the parties were informed that
X suffered from exomphalos, a birth defect of the abdominal (belly) wall that
eventually required surgery after birth. Madame also apparently had a high-risk
pregnancy that forced her to take a medical leave from work.

[
15
]

Given the immediate family situation and the
fact that Madame’s mother and Monsieur’s parents all lived in City A, the
parties decided to temporarily relocate to this city in September of 2018. X
was born in City A on [...] 2018 and was immediately taken for surgery the next
day. The operation was a success.

[
16
]

Following X’s birth the relationship between the
parties began to deteriorate rapidly and Madame officially left Monsieur on 21
August 2019. She filed for divorce before the Quebec Superior Court 7 days
later, indicating that there was a breakdown of the marriage due to physical
and mental cruelty.

[
17
]

At the same time, by way of provisional and
interim measures, Madame asked for, as it was referred to then, sole legal and
physical custody of the child and permission from the court to relocate to
Ontario to resume employment upon the termination of her maternity leave on 24
November 2019.

[
18
]

Madame’s application for provisional and interim
measures and Monsieur’s amended application for provisional measures for
custody of the child was heard by Mongeon J. on 5 December 2019.

[
19
]

In a decision delivered two weeks later, Mongeon
J., granted custody to X’s mother allowing her to move to City B with him and he
granted progressive access rights to his father, one day per week from 9 a.m.
to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday during the months of January and February 2020 and
two days per week, again from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., during the months of March and
April 2020.

[
20
]

In granting Madame’s request to return to
Ontario with X, Mongeon J. noted :

[100]    Having considered all
issues, considering the very young age of the child, the fact that the
Plaintiff is the principal and primary care giver of X, the fact that she is
still breastfeeding him as well as the necessity to maintain the human
surroundings in which the child is presently evolving,
I find that the
Plaintiff should be entrusted with the exclusive custody of X and allowed to
return to City B to pursue her professional career at [Company A]
.

[101]
This finding is made in
the context of a provisional order to remain in force until final judgment of
divorce in first instance
.

[102]
The Defendant is
entitled to appropriate access rights
. He proposes the following in the
event of an order authorizing the Plaintiff to return to City B. […]

[103]    [The proposal of the
Defendant] makes little sense or no sense in a situation where the mother is
still breastfeeding.

[104]    This proposal confines the
child in City A under the complete control of the Defendant and depriving a
very young infant from daily contact with his primary care giver.  This is the
antithesis of protecting the best interest of the child.

[105]    This proposal also shows
that the Defendant’s attitude is not in line with the reality of the child’s
life experience. It would be a shock to his system and in any event it would
never happen because the mother would never leave City A if his custody and/or
access scheme would be retained.

[106]    The Plaintiff suggests the
following scenario […].

[107]    This scenario is not
perfect and will need to be modulated.

[108]
The Defendant’s
attitude towards the Plaintiff herself may be subject to criticism but this
does not mean that the baby will be unsafe or improperly looked after once he
is under the care of his father
.

[109]
The hearing before me
did not adequately cover the question of access by the Defendant in the context
of the Plaintiff being in City B with the child
.

[110]    The Defendant has limited
his access proposal in the context of the child staying in City A. It would be
unfair for me to determine, on a provisional basis, access rights for the
Defendant to be exercised in City B without hearing him and without further analysis
of the impact on the child’s residence outside of City A.

[111]
An additional hearing
would therefore have to be scheduled
where both parties will be offered all
the latitude necessary to examine this question and obtain appropriate access
orders.

[112]    In the meantime, I will
retain, on an interim basis, the access offered by the Plaintiff but for a
maximum period of four months, that is, until April 30, 2020.

[113]    I will also increase the
number of access days to per two week for March and April 2020.

[114]
Before April 30, 2020
,
the parties will either have to agree on the question of the Defendant’s access
or proceed by way of Motion and obtain judgment.

[Underlining is mine]

[
21
]

On 14 February 2020, Monsieur’s lawyers filed a
notice of presentation for further access rights to be determined on 28 April
2020. It is not exactly clear what, if anything, happened to that notice. The court
record indicates, however, that on 10 June 2020, Madame’s lawyers filed an
application pursuant to, among others, articles 3093 and 3135 of the C.C.Q. to
refer this entire court file or alternatively the aspects in it relating to X
to the Ontario Superior Court of Justice.

[
22
]

Six days later, Monsieur’s lawyers filed an
application seeking access rights to X every other weekend from 9 a.m. on
Thursday to 5 p.m. on Sunday at the arrivals area of the Toronto Pearson
Airport and 7 consecutive days for the end of the year period from 23 December
at 9 a.m. to 30 December 2020 at 5 p.m. or alternatively from this last date at
9 a.m. to 6 January 2021 at 5 p.m. with the exchange to take place again at the
Toronto Pearson Airport. At the hearing before me, Monsieur verbally changed
this request to equal parenting time, asking for “one week, one week”.

[
23
]

Monsieur’s lawyers also sought confirmation of equal
parental rights with respect to, among other matters, religious, health, and place
of residence, education and choice of school questions relating to X. This is
something for the Ontario Superior Court of Justice to address going forward.

[
24
]

Due in part to the pandemic, on 30 September
2020, both the application of Madame dated 10 June and that of Monsieur dated
16 June 2020 (including presumably the earlier one of 28 April 2020), where
fixed by Beaugé J. to be heard before me on 17 and 18 March 2021, with an
indication that Madame’s “
forum non conveniens
” application ought to
proceed first.

[
25
]

Beaugé J. also renewed Mongeon J.’s provisional
and interim measures judgment until the end of the hearing before me. At end of
the hearing of 18 March 2021, I renewed that judgment until the release of this
decision.

ANALYSIS

[
26
]

Concerned about, among other things, costs and efficacy
in these proceedings and given X’s very young age and the fact that the parties
reside in two different provinces, at the opening of the 17 March hearing and
on a few other occasions during the course of the two-day hearing, I asked the
parties whether they wished the Court to conclusively address all remaining
economic and other issues between them and pronounce divorce. This would have
brought final closure to the minor remaining issues, if any, pending before the
Quebec Superior Court.

[
27
]

Neither Monsieur nor Madame followed up on such
a proposal, although both indicated that there were insignificant economic (and
certainly no family patrimony) issues remaining between them. Even though unfortunate
for costs and resource purposes, I will now address the only two issues raised before
me – transfer of proceedings to Ontario and additional parenting time for
Monsieur. I will examine these issues in the order they were presented to me as
per the decision of Beaugé J.

Transfer
of proceedings

[
28
]

Madame argues that section 6 (1) of the
Act

and articles 3093, 3135 and 3142 C.C.Q. all militate in favour of the Quebec
Superior Court declining jurisdiction in favour of the Ontario Superior Court
of Justice. Monsieur disagrees, holds firmly on to the divorce proceedings
pending in this province and argues in favour of the continued competence of this
Court.

[
29
]

Pursuant to
section 6 (1)
of the
Act
, if
an application for a child parenting order is sought in a divorce proceeding in
Quebec, such as in this case, and the child of the marriage – X – in respect of
whom the order is sought is
habitually resident
in Ontario, the Quebec
Superior Court
may
, on application by his mother or father or on the court’s
own motion, transfer the proceeding to a court in Ontario.

[
30
]

In examining this issue in this case, it is
important to keep in mind Mongeon J.’s December 2019 decision that explicitly allows
Madame to return to City B and permits Monsieur to present an application to
the Quebec Superior Court for additional parenting time with X.

Section 6 (1)
of the

Act

[
31
]

The keystone of section 6 (1) is the
habitual
residence
of the child and the court’s duty in identifying it. If that
residence, which has intentionally not been defined in the
Act
, is in a
province other than the one where a divorce or corollary relief is pending, the
competent court where the proceeding is pending has the discretion, but is not
obliged, to transfer the proceeding to the competent court where the child has
his or her habitual residence.

[
32
]

In addition to bringing the
Act
more in
line with the terminology used in international law and certain provinces, the
purpose behind using habitual residence instead of the former notion, “most
substantially connected”, is the best interests of the child now explicitly but
not exhaustively legislated under
section 16
of the
Act
.  The better the
court is positioned in understanding the section 16 factors relating to child, or
said differently, the closer the court is in better understanding the child’s
life and surrounding circumstances, the better positioned the court is in addressing
the parenting order requested.

[
33
]

For good reasons, the
Act
does not define
“habitual residence”, which is a concept that appears to be neither frequently
resorted to under common law nor covered in the C.C.Q. that principally refers
to the notion of domicile. Under the C.C.Q., article 75 defines the domicile of
a person, for the exercise of his or her civil rights, as that person’s
principal establishment. Article 76 states that change of domicile is effected
by a person establishing his or her residence in another place with the
intention of making it that person’s principal establishment. Intention is to
be determined based on the declarations of the person and the circumstances of
the case. And finally, article 77 in turn defines the residence of a person as
the place where he or she ordinarily resides. If a person has more than one
residence, that person’s principal residence is considered in establishing his
domicile.

[
34
]

It appears on the other hand that the term
habitual residence has a continental European heritage and was imported into
the various laws of Canada through likely the influence of the various Hague
Conventions and Uniform Legislative Conferences. A good example is use of the
term “habitually resident” found in article 7 (2) of The Hague
Convention on
Jurisdiction, Applicable Law, Recognition, Enforcement and Co-operation in
Respect of Parental Responsibility and Measure for the Protection of Children
,
[9]
which convention is to be given
the force of law in Canada through
section 30.1 (1)
of the
Act
.

[
35
]

Article 7 (2) is identical to article 3 of The Hague

Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction
[10]
that was meticulously examined
by the Supreme Court in 2018
[11]
.
In that case the central question before the Court was how an application judge
should approach the determination of habitual residence under article 3 of the Convention
[12]
.

[
36
]

In
Balev
, after examining the three
different approaches submitted to it for determining a child’s habitual
residence under article 3, the majority of the Supreme Court concluded that the
hybrid approach – and not the parental intention approach or the child-centered
approach – should be adopted in Canada
[13]
.

[
37
]

Writing for the majority, Chief Justice
McLachlin, as she then was, had this to say about the determination of habitual
residence under article 3 of the
Child Abduction Convention
:

[43]      On the hybrid approach to
habitual residence, the application judge determines the focal point of the
child’s life – “the family and social environment in which its life has
developed” – immediately prior to the removal or retention […]. The judge
considers all relevant links and circumstances – the child’s links to and
circumstances in country A; the circumstances of the child’s move from country
A to country B; and the child’s links to and circumstances in country B.

[44]      Considerations include
“the duration, regularity, conditions and reasons for the child’s stay in the
territory of a Member State and the child’s nationality […]. No single factor
dominates the analysis; rather, the application judge should consider the
entirety of the circumstances […]. Relevant considerations may vary according
to the age of the child concerned: where the child is an infant, “the
environment of a young child is essentially a family environment, determined by
the reference person(s) with whom the child lives, by whom the child is in fact
looked after and taken care of” […].

[45]      The circumstances of the
parents, including their intentions, may be important, particularly in the case
of infants and young children […]. However, recent cases caution against
over-reliance on parental intention. The Court of Justice of the European Union
stated […] that parental intention “can also be taken into account, where that
intention is manifested by certain tangible steps such as the purchase or lease
of a residence” […]. It “cannot as a general rule by itself be crucial to the
determination of the habitual residence of a child […] but constitutes an
‘indicator’ capable of complementing a body of other consistent evidence” […].
The role of parental intention in the determination of habitual residence
“depends on the circumstances specific to each individual case” […].

[…]

[47]      The hybrid approach is
“fact-bound, practical, and unencumbered with rigid rules, formulas, or
presumptions” […]. It requires the application judge to look to the entirety of
the child’s situation. While courts allude to factors or considerations that
tend to recur, there is no legal test for habitual residence and the list of
potentially relevant factors is not closed. The temptation “to overlay the
factual concept of habitual residence with legal constructs” must be resisted
[…].

[
38
]

In my view, for the sake of uniformity and
consistency, the determination of habitual residence under
section 6 (1)
of the

Act
must take place pursuant to the same directions and criteria laid
out in
Balev
with, of course, any necessary adaptations. Put
differently, national law can inspire itself from the guidance offered by the
Supreme Court in an international context and apply it malleably and
interchangeably domestically.

[
39
]

In this case the only adaptation required to the
roadmap offered in
Balev
before applying it to a section 6 (1)
application is the moment in time when the application judge should consider
the factors enumerated. The reference to countries A and B can simply be read
as provinces A and B as, again, in the context of a section 6 (1) application there
is no question of international abduction.

[
40
]

Accordingly, in an application for a parenting
order, the most appropriate moment to consider the above factors is when the
application is heard. In addition, the determination of habitual residence must
be fact specific and malleable and the
court must focus on the child,
not the parents, and consider past experience but remain open to future
intentions of both parents. While obvious, it should be recalled that a person
can only have one habitual residence.

[
41
]

Article 3093 C.C.Q. requires that custody of a child be
governed by the law of his or her domicile or principal establishment. Article 3135
states that even though a Quebec authority has jurisdiction to hear a dispute,
it may, exceptionally and on an application of a party, decline jurisdiction if
it considers that the authorities of another jurisdiction are in a better
position to decide the dispute. Finally, article 3142 provides that Quebec
authorities have jurisdiction to decide the custody of a child provided he or
she is domiciled in Quebec.

[
42
]

Articles 3093 and 3142 go hand in hand. A Quebec authority
will not render a custody or parenting time decision as it is now referred to
regarding a child that is not domiciled in Quebec and subject to Quebec law.
Not much ink needs to be spilled on this issue. In any event, Madame is not
arguing that the Quebec Superior Court is not competent to hear Monsieur’s
additional parenting time application in the context of the divorce proceeding
pending in Quebec.

[
43
]

Rather, Madame’s position is that the Ontario Superior Court
of Justice is in a better position to decide the various disagreements between
the parties. According to her, she and X now reside in Ontario, she works in
Ontario and X will be attending preschool in that province soon
[14]
.
According to Madame, whether examined under
section 6 (1)
of the
Act
or

article 3135
C.C.Q., the result is the same. The Ontario Superior Court of
Justice is the better or more convenient forum.

Article 3135 C.C.Q.

[
44
]

Article 3135 codifies the doctrine of
forum non conveniens

under Quebec private international law which, given its draconian consequences,
is reserved for exceptional cases. In adopting in a family law context in 2019
the criteria put forward by Pidgeon J., as he then was at the Court of Appeal
in 1998
[15]
, the Supreme Court
directs the application judge to consider the following ten criteria
[16]
,
among others, before applying the exception.

[
45
]

The Supreme Court
reiterates that none of these criteria are determinative on their own, the list
is not exhaustive, others may be added depending on the circumstances and the
weight to be given to any of them must be assessed globally in the context of the
specific case
[17]
.

(1)

the place of residence of the parties and of lay and expert
witnesses;

(2)

the location of the physical evidence;

(3)

the place of formation and performance of the contract that
resulted in the   application;

(4)

the existence and subject of an action instituted in another
country and        the stage already reached in that action;

(5)

the location of the defendant’s assets;

(6)

the law applicable to the dispute;

(7)

the advantages the plaintiff would have in the chosen forum;

(8)

the interests of justice;

(9)

the interests of the two parties; and

(10)

the eventual need for an exemplification
proceeding in the other country.

[
46
]

According to the Supreme Court, these criteria
should be examined from a procedural perspective, “because what is at issue is
which of the two fora is in the best position to hear the case.”
[18]

[
47
]

I take from the above that in a case where the
Act

applies because the parties are married, the transfer of a proceeding where a
parenting order has been applied for will require consideration of
both

section 6 (1) of the
Act
and article 3135 C.C.Q.

[
48
]

If the requirements of section 6 (1) are not
met, there is no need to proceed with the criteria set out in article 3135
C.C.Q. This approach best ensures the harmonized national application of the
Act
.
Section 6 (1) will apply universally across Canada and common law principles
will address the criteria found under article 3135 C.C.Q. case law.

[
49
]

For reasons that follow, in this case, I agree
with Madame that going forward, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice will be better
positioned to address any parenting order issues relating to X. I also agree
with Madame that, at this stage, the Quebec Superior Court can on a provisional
basis address the issues raised by Monsieur in his 16 June 2020 application.

[
50
]

Again, had the parties, and particularly
Monsieur, agreed to finalize the divorce proceeding pending before this Court,
I could have also finally disposed of that issue for their mutual benefit.

Habitual Residence

[
51
]

By analogy to the factors that were put forth by
the Supreme Court in
Balev
, the determination of the habitual residence
of X will require consideration of, among others, the following non-exhaustive
elements: his family and social environment at the time the application was
heard, his links to Ontario and Quebec, the duration, regularity, conditions
and reasons for his stay in Ontario, and finally, considering his very young
and tender age, the circumstances of his parents, including their past and
future intentions.

[
52
]

X was born in City A on [...] 2018 and lived in
this city until 1 January 2020 when following the judgment of Mongeon J., he
was allowed to relocate to Ontario with his mother. X now lives in City D, a
town in southern Ontario halfway between City B and City E. City D is part of
the City B Area.

[
53
]

Before the pandemic, X attended [School A], a
child care centre located in City D for a brief period of time and he is
currently on the waiting list of [pre-school A], a French language child centre
to potentially start there in September of 2021
[19]
. If accepted, X will attend
pre-kindergarten from Monday to Friday.

[
54
]

Except during the year 2019, X’s mother has
lived and worked in Ontario since 2016. She currently works in the healthcare
private insurance environment relating to the opioid dependency drugs and she
has no intention of returning to City A. Madame earns a comfortable living,
about $150,000 a year, with a possibility of a bonus.

[
55
]

Although she is domiciled in the province of
Quebec, has owned for the past forty years and continues to own a home in City
A, X’s maternal grandmother also temporarily resides in Ontario in order to be
near her daughter and help with looking after her grandson. Madame’s mother’s
partner on the other hand lives in City A. X’s mother is his principal
caretaker and the person on whom he counts most daily for security, love and
care.

[
56
]

Madame is an only child and she has no
relationship with X’s maternal grandfather – her own father – whose whereabouts
are unknown to her. Madame has an aunt in City A who has three children. Two
live in City A and one in Alaska. Madame also has three uncles, only one of
whom lives in City A.  Like the majority of children his age, X is also being
followed by a pediatrician in Ontario.

[
57
]

X’s father lives in City A and looks after
properties that he owns. He earns approximately $30,000 a year and does not
wish or intend to seek other employment, because it may interfere with his time
with X. He prefers instead to keep his time flexible and available to travel to
Ontario to see his son.

[
58
]

Presently, as provided in Mongeon J.’s judgment,
Monsieur travels to Ontario to see X two times a week from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.  In
order to spend more time with his son, Monsieur is ready and willing to secure
a dwelling in the City B Area. Finally, X’s paternal grandparents who are in
their sixties, Monsieur’s two sisters and their families – one of Monsieur’s
sisters has two children – and many of X’s relatives on his father’s side live
in City A.

[
59
]

Based on all of the above facts, X’s personal
and family situation globally, and his very young age in particular, I am of
the view that X habitually resides in Ontario. Principally, X’s mother who is
his primary caregiver lives there, his permanent home where he spends all of
his time currently is there, and he plans to attend pre-school there. This
conclusion is also in conformity with the conclusion reached by Mongeon J., in
his judgment.

[
60
]

The question that needs to be examined now is
whether the Ontario Superior Court of Justice is better placed to address the
parenting time issues relating to X. In my view, the answer is yes. The
Oppenheim
-factors
approved by the Supreme Court support such a conclusion.

[
61
]

Madame and X are both physically located in
Ontario. Monsieur regularly and frequently travels there to see X. He also
intends to secure a dwelling in that province in order to spend more quality
time with X. The fact that Madame’s lead family lawyers are in Ontario is also
relevant. In this case personality and serious communication difficulties
between the parties at the time of exchange of X as ordered by Mongeon J.,
required Madame to retain Ontario lawyers. The law applicable to the parties
and their particular situation, the
Act
, is equally applicable in both
provinces`

[
62
]

The fact that a divorce proceeding is pending in
Quebec and Monsieur is holding on to that proceeding as a possible anchor in
maintaining the conflict between the parties alive in this province is also of
no support to Monsieur.
Section 6 (1)
of the
Act
explicitly foresees
such a possibility and even offers an answer to it by allowing the application
judge adequate discretion to address it on a case by case basis. Moreover, the
parties do not seem to have any significant economic issues pending before them
that warrants the continued competence of the Quebec courts once the divorce
judgment has been rendered.

[
63
]

Finally, the best interests of X, considering
his age, habitual residence, and the presence of his primary caregiver in
Ontario militate for a transfer of all future parental issues to the Ontario
Superior Court of Justice. Going forward many of the issues relating to X and
his development will most likely be Ontario-centric, among them for example,
the choice of daycare or prekindergarten for X, the selection of eventually a
kindergarten and elementary school for him and when again possible, the choice
of social, sport and other daily activities. For the sake of X and all other
children, the Court hopes this will come soon.

[
64
]

Of course, in reaching this decision, I am not
unaware of the disparity between the income levels of the parties – a fact
which at least in part can be attributed to the deliberate choice of Monsieur
not working in the past when the parties first moved to Ontario in 2016 for
Madame to gain initial work experience and Monsieur’s current decision not to
work so that he may have more time available to see his son – and the impact
this decision may have on the overall administration of justice.

[
65
]

This said, as I indicated earlier, based on

section 6 (1)
of the
Act
, on the judgment of Mongeon J. and the fact
that there is currently a divorce application pending before this Court, I am
prepared to provide the parties with an interim judgement that will remain in
force until
4 October 2021.

[
66
]

At that point, unless the parties agree
otherwise, or reach an amicable solution which incontrovertibly will be in both
of their interests, one or the other will have to seek the assistance of the
Ontario Superior Court of Justice. One of the, if not the principal, axis of
the
Act
is to give primacy to the best interests of children. In this
case, in my view, the Ontario courts will be better placed to intervene in the
parental and other issues relating to X.

Additional Parenting time for
Monsieur

[
67
]

Monsieur asks for equal parenting time with X
when he has not to date had the opportunity to keep X overnight. In Monsieur’s
mind, X is also old enough to be able to live with him during alternate weeks
between City A and City D.

[
68
]

I disagree with Monsieur.

[
69
]

Monsieur’s proposal or request is neither
realistic nor reasonable. X is simply too young to suddenly be away from his
primary caretaker, his mother, for seven consecutive days. He has not so far
spent any nights away from her.

[
70
]

In the case of all children, and especially very
young children, parenting time is precious time that can be spent in the care
of their mother, father or the person who stands or intends to stand in their
place. That person must be ready, willing and able to care for the child. The
best individuals to address the quantity and quality of parenting time are
parents. They are the ones who best understand the needs of the child. If
parents or those who stand in the place of parents are not able to or choose
not to make such decisions in the best interests of the child, the court will
fulfill that role.

[
71
]

In that scenario, the
Act
prescribes that
in allocating parenting time, a court must give effect to the principle that “a
child should have as much time with each spouse as is consistent with the best
interests of the child.” The
Act
also provides that in determining the
best interests of a child, “the court shall not take into consideration the
past conduct of any person unless that conduct is relevant to the exercise of
their parenting time, decision-making responsibility or contact with the child
under a contact order.”

[
72
]

The
Act
enumerates a variety of
non-exhaustive factors that are to be considered in seeking to identify the best
interests of a child. Among them are the needs of the child given his or her
age and stage of development, the nature and strength of the child’s
relationship with the parenting order applicant, the child’s grandparents or
others who play and important part in the child’s life, the parenting order
applicant and the other spouse’s willingness to support one another in the
child developing a relationship with the other, the history of child care and
plans for such a care, the child’s cultural, linguistic, religious and
spiritual upbringing and heritage, the ability of the person seeking a
parenting order to care for and meet the needs of the child as well as
communicate with the other spouse on matters affecting the child, any history
of family violence and its impact on the ability to care for and meet the needs
of the child, any civil or criminal proceeding that may be relevant for the
safety, security and well-being of the child.

[
73
]

When considering these factors, the
Act

explicitly requires that primary consideration be given to the child’s
physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being. I will,
therefore, examine each of these in more detail below before reaching a
conclusion concerning the additional parenting time requested by Monsieur.

[
74
]

Before going any further, it is important to
recall that presently, Monsieur travels to Ontario every week on Wednesdays to
pick up X from his mother in the parking lot of a supermarket on Thursday
morning at 9 a.m. to then drop him off again at that same location at 5 p.m. He
does the same thing the next day.

[
75
]

During the time that X is with his father,
Monsieur explains that he takes him back to his hotel room to play, look at
books, feed him – at times with Greek food that Monsieur’s mother has prepared
in advance and sent for X – give him a nap and then take him back to his
mother.

[
76
]

This kind of arrangement, which has already
lasted for more than a year is
not
in X’s best interests.

[
77
]

Madame is of the view that Monsieur is simply
not ready to share equal parenting time with her and that in any event X is too
young for such an arrangement, especially taking into account Monsieur’s
current permanent residence in City A. Madame is also of the view that Monsieur
needs to work on and improve a number of things, including his communication
skills with her concerning X, before he is given more time with the child.

[
78
]

In this regard, among others, Madame
specifically refers to an incident where X was with his father during the day
and upon picking him up and placing him in his car seat Madame noticed that he
was visibly unconformable and in much pain. Madame’s immediate investigation of
the issue at the SickKids Hospital Emergency Department in Toronto led to the
diagnosis of a buckle fracture of distal end of left radius.

[
79
]

According to Madame, it is not the injury itself
that is a source of concern for her regarding X. As she explains, X is a little
boy and he will likely have other mishaps. Madame’s preoccupation is that
either Monsieur did not notice that there was something wrong with the child or
he actually did and decided not to say anything to her for fear of reprisal. In
either case, Madame submits, there is cause for concern – communication
difficulties between the parties is so poor that it risks seriously causing
harm to the child.

[
80
]

Madame also refers to Monsieur filming her every
time that X is exchanged between them. Monsieur explains that he was told by
Ontario police to do it so as to protect himself. This way he adds, he cannot
be accused of anything. Madame’s explanation of this continuing gesture is that
Monsieur knows that filming aggravates her, so he does it to make a point.

[
81
]

Finally, although Madame refers to certain past
incidents of violence, she explains that she does
not
wish to use this
factor as means of preventing Monsieur to see his son. According to Madame, her
marital relationship with Monsieur was wrought with verbal, emotional and
physical abuse to the point that she had no choice but to leave the family home
with her child and no belongings.

[
82
]

Madame also does not object to Monsieur
gradually spending more and more time with X but notes that she is gravely
scarred by Monsieur’s past behaviour and is concerned that their communication
and personality difficulties will continue to have a negative long-lasting
impact on their child.

[
83
]

Before me, Monsieur tries to downplay the
incidents referred to by Madame and ultimately states that he is prepared to do
anything and accept any arrangement to spend more time with his son, including
securing a dwelling in Ontario and travelling there as much as required to be
near him.

[
84
]

In order to presumably bolster his credibility,
two weeks after the close of a two-day hearing, on 30 March 2021, Monsieur
wrote to the Court asking that the proceedings be reopened so that he may file
a letter that he had just received from his Ontario criminal counsel. That
letter, dated 29 March 2021, reads in part as follows:

I am counsel for Mr. A. M. for
criminal charges he was facing in City B.

On Thursday June 18, 2020 Mr. M.
was charged in City B with a sole count of assault. The charge related to an
allegation of domestic assault made by Ms. J. B..

This charge proceeded in the
Ontario Court of Justice at College Park in Toronto. I am writing to advise
that on March 26, 2021 in courtroom #505 at the College Park courthouse
the
charge against Mr. M. was withdrawn
at the request of the assistant crown
prosecutor Kaely Hebert.

[…]

[Underlining is mine]

[
85
]

In response, on 31 March 2021, Madame’s lawyer
asked the Court for indulgence to have her Ontario criminal lawyer examine the
court transcript to obtain more clarity on the statement “the charge against
Mr. M. was withdrawn”.

[
86
]

In giving the parties the opportunity to
complete the record regarding this issue, I reminded them at the time that this
would have an impact on the delivery date of this judgment, and of course,
their benefit of the directions set out in it. Both parties wrote back
indicating that they understood. The above exchanges and the Court’s
assignments in the interim explain the month or so delay in delivering this
judgment. Ideally, if the parties had not sought a re-opening of the
proceedings, this decision would have been released earlier.

[
87
]

Be that as it may, on 9 April 2021, Madame’s
Ontario criminal counsel, offered additional insight regarding the withdrawal
of charges against Monsieur. Upon receipt of that letter, Monsieur’s lawyer
raised a hearsay caution against certain paragraphs in that letter. Monsieur’s
lawyer also stated that all comments offered by Madame’s Ontario criminal
lawyer that reach beyond the italic citation are nothing but her own inductions
and speculations
[20]
.
The letter of 9 April 2021, reads in part, as follows:

I am writing to you regarding the
withdrawal of A. M.’s City B charge of domestic assault. I am counsel to the
victim, Ms. B., having offered her legal guidance in the criminal process in
City B. The charge against Mr. M. was marked withdrawn on March 26, 2021 […].

Ms. Kaely Hebert was Crown counsel
who had carriage of the City B prosecution. The period of time from the date of
the assault to the date of Mr. M.’s arrest was outside the 6-month summary
conviction limitation period. As a result of that, the matter had to be pursued
by Indictment which would require prosecution in the Superior Court of Justice.
A public decision was made not to proceed by Indictment, due to the massive delays
at the Superior Court because of the pandemic. As a result, the Crown agreed to

Ms. Hebert was not the Crown
appearing in courtroom #505 on the day that Mr. M.’s matter was in court. As a
result, the day prior to the withdrawal of the charge, Ms. Hebert entered a
note into the Crown’s portal called “Scope” to notify Crown counsel appearing
what was to be done in Mr. M.’s matter and why. Ms. Hebert’s note is as
follows:

“K. Hebert
(03/25/2021 03:43 PM):

to 505:
PLEASE WITHDRAW CHARGES

He
successfully completed Just For Today domestic violence counselling. I accepted

period and I was not going by indictment. He still has o/s charges in City A
with the same vic that will be going to trial soon.
”

It is for the
above reasons that Mr. M.’s matter was withdrawn in City B. […]

[
88
]

Monsieur’s hearsay caution or objection, if in
fact it is one, is dismissed, especially in light of the Crown counsel, Ms.
Kaely Herbert’s email confirmation on 12 April 2021 that the letter of April 9
“accurately reflects the Crown’s consideration in withdrawing the charges.”

[
89
]

Despite the above, Madame’s position concerning
the benefit that parenting time and possibly additional parenting time with his
father would offer X remained unwavered. Madame is to be commended for such an
approach, which is precisely the type of maturity and introspection that is
required of X’s parents to ensure his best interests.

[90]

Again, because before me Madame explicitly
indicated that she did not want her past personal difficulties with Monsieur
to interfere with him establishing a relationship with X, and moreover, that
all she was looking for was for Monsieur to reconsider and readjust his
communication methods and behaviour with her, I will refrain from expanding
on this issue any further save for the brief comments that I will offer
below. Again, I commend Madame for her courage.

[91]

This brings me now to Monsieur’s request for
additional parenting time with X, which Madame, as indicated earlier, does
not really object to but calls for caution in light of X’s age, Monsieur’s
experience in looking after his son, and their past and continuing
communication difficulties.

Parenting Time Schedule

[92]

Based on an overall evaluation of the facts
and evidence before me, and keeping in mind the factors enumerated in
section
16 (1)
of the
Act
, and in particular, X’s physical, emotional and
psychological safety, security and well-being, I am of the view that on an
interim basis, X should benefit from additional time with his father as
described below, assuming that the following conditions and safeguards are observed
and respected.

[93]

Beginning on 1 July 2021 – I will come back to
the remaining days in the month of May and the month of June momentarily – if
Monsieur has rented a furnished or to be furnished dwelling in the City B
Area, as he indicated he was open to doing in order to have more time with X,
and provides a copy of the corresponding lease to Madame’s Ontario lawyers, X
may start spending Friday and Saturday nights with his father every other
weekend as follows.

[94]

X will be with his father on July 2 and 3,
July 16 and 17 and then again July 30 and 31. Monsieur and Madame will
continue to exchange X at the same location as they have thus far – the
parking lot of [Supermarket A] located at [...] in City D, Ontario. Madame
will give X to his father at 9 a.m. on Friday and she will pick him up at 9
a.m. on Sunday.

[95]

The drop off and pick up will be from car to
car. Upon arrival at the usual supermarket site Monsieur will text his exact
location to Madame, who will then park nearby and physically take X to Monsieur’s
car. Madame will place X in his car seat in Monsieur’s car at drop off and
she will take him out of the car seat at pick up. On both occasions, Monsieur
will remain in his car and in the driver’s seat and ideally not film the
exchange as he has been doing.

[96]

Seeing that the above events will be taking
place in another jurisdiction, and Monsieur indicates that he was explicitly
advised by local authorities in Ontario “to do what he is doing”, I hesitate
to go any further than strongly recommending to him that he should consider a
different approach and refrain from filming the exchanges of X.

[97]

If despite the above, Monsieur continues to
film the exchanges, that will be an issue for the Ontario Superior Court of
Justice to address. If the exchange was taking place in Quebec, I would not
hesitate to order Monsieur to put an end to it, for among other reasons, X’s
best interests. Considering X’s young age, it would be best for him, if only
for safety reasons, if his parents both focussed on his physical and emotional
well-being during these exchanges.

[98]

During the weeks that X would not be spending
two nights with his father, except in the month of August, Monsieur would
benefit from the same arrangement as in the past. In other words, X would be
able to see his father on Thursdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and then again on
Fridays during the same hours. The exchanges would take place at the same
location and in the manner as prescribed above.

[99]

Assuming that X is benefitting from the
additional time with his father, starting on 1 August 2021, X may stay with
his father during 5 consecutive nights but
not
two consecutive weeks
during that month. If X’s parents are unable to agree on mutually convenient
dates, the weeks that X will be with his father will be from Monday, August 9
at 9 a.m. until Saturday, August 14 at 9 a.m., and then again Monday, August
23 at 9 a.m. until Saturday, August 28 at 9 a.m.

[100]

Once again the exchanges will take place in
the same manner as described above. These two non-consecutive weeks will
provide X with an opportunity to spend quality time, not only with his
father, but also perhaps during one of the two weeks with his paternal
grandparents, if the current public health conditions and applicable local,
provincial and national directives permit them to travel to Ontario to see X.
Based on Monsieur’s testimony, X’s paternal grandparents are young and
healthy enough to make the necessary arrangements to visit him in Ontario.

[101]

The parties will revert back to the
July-inspired schedule in the month of September and X will again be with his
father on September 3 and 4, 17 and 18 and then again on October 1 and 2. The
parties may continue this same arrangement going forward unless of course
they agree otherwise or seek further direction from the Ontario Court of
Justice on or after 4 October 2021. If with the agreement of the parties, X
has started pre-school in September, rather than from 9 a.m. to 9 a.m., X
will be with his father from after pre-school to 5 p.m. on Sunday.

[102]

In the interim, during the month of June, X
may start spending one night a week every other week with his father if
Monsieur provides the contact details of the hotel, apartment or other
location where he would be temporarily staying during that month. During the
weeks in the month of June that X would not be spending one night with his
father, Monsieur would benefit from the same arrangement as in the past. In
other words, X would be able to see his father on Thursday from 9 a.m. to 5
p.m. and then again on Friday during the same hours. If in September, with
the agreement of his parents, X is attending pre-school, these hours will
change to after preschool and 7 p.m. On those days, Monsieur would be able to
pick up X at his preschool.

[103]

If the parties are unable to agree in advance
on what days during the month of June X would spend an evening with his
father, that day would change from week to week. During the first week in
June, the sleeping night would be Friday, June 4 to June 5, and the following
sleepover would be Thursday, June 17 to June 18. The exchanges again will
take place according to the same manner set out above. For example, on 4 June
2021, Monsieur would pick up X at 9 a.m. and he would take him back to Madame
at 9 a.m. the following day.

[104]

The arrangement for the remaining days in May
shall be as ordered before this judgment – in other words, on Thursday, 27
May 2021 and Friday, 28 May 2021, X will be with his father from 9 a.m. to 5
p.m. There will be no sleepover in May.

[105]

The above arrangements, which will remain in
place until Monday, 4 October 2021 unless the parties mutually agree
otherwise or the Ontario Superior Court of Justice intervenes in the interim,
are in my view, in the best interests of X, considering his physical,
emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being.

[106]

They also take into consideration, among
others, X’s young age, needs, the nature and strength of his development with
his parents and grandparents, in particular, his paternal grandparents, his
history of care, X’s cultural and linguistic heritage, and the parties
willingness to care and meet his needs and their ability and willingness to
communicate and cooperate with one another on matters affecting him, keeping
in mind the impact of such factors as family violence and its effect on X’s
emotional and psychological state.

[107]

Finally, they squarely respect the principle
set forth in
section 16 (6)
of the
Act
which requires that the Court
allocate parenting time based on time with each spouse that the court
determines to be “consistent with the best interests of the child”.

[108]

X is barely over two years old and so far, he
has spent the majority of his time with his primary caregiver who is his
mother. He has also never had any sleepovers with his father. X’s best
interests, therefore, require that he gradually start to spend overnights
with his father while at the same time, at the beginning at least, not being
far from his mother.

[109]

The ability for X to initially spend one
evening, then two and then eventually 5 during the month of August will not
only gradually establish a more permanent bond between him and his father,
but hopefully allow him during his stays with his father to spend more time
with his paternal grandparents and down the road his father’s family so as to
maintain his Greek heritage.

Violence

[110]

Even though for the right reasons, Madame’s
Quebec lawyers do not place much emphasis in this application on the issue of
violence other than to say that it is “the proverbial elephant in the room”
and the Court should be cognisant of it, as indicated earlier, I will open a
brief parentheses here to make a few remarks.

[111]

It is important to recall that the
Act

requires the Court to examine the impact of family violence on, among other
things, the appropriateness of making an order that would require “persons in
respect of whom the order would apply to cooperate on issues affecting the
child.” In considering the impact of any family violence, the Court is
required to take into consideration, among others, the nature and seriousness
of the violence and when it occurred, the physical, emotional and
psychological harm or risk of harm to the child and any compromise to the
safety of the child.

[112]

In this case, concerned about her well-being,
Madame asked the Court for permission not to reveal her address in Ontario
for the purpose of being sworn in. The background of this, as explained by
Madame’s lawyer, is found in Madame’s sworn statement dated 28 August 2019,
in which she explains, among other things, that 7 days earlier, she “finally
built up the courage” and left Monsieur because she “could not take his
abuse, both physical and verbal, any longer.” She describes in that statement
that Monsieur was dominating and controlling, that he had tried by various
means to manipulate her into being dependent on him, that he had insulted her
by calling her names, and tried to continuously undermine her.

[113]

The clinical notes from Herzl GMF (Family
Medicine Group), a walk-in clinic located in the vicinity of the Jewish
General Hospital in Montreal and affiliated with McGill University’s Faculty
of Medicine during the months of January and February 2019 indicate that
Madame was complaining about her husband not being supportive, making her cry
every day, trying to control or manipulate her, threatening to divorce her,
and on one occasion kicking her in the back.

[114]

While it is not for this Court to comment on
the veracity and gravity of the above facts because firstly, Madame’s lawyer
has chosen not to address them in any detail and moreover, because another
more appropriate forum is or may be examining them, it is relevant for this
Court to consider them in making an order for pickup and drop off in respect
to the parenting time that is being ordered in relation to X.

[115]

Here, Madame’s continuous concerns about
principally her own well-being prevents her from sharing her home address
with Monsieur, which situation in turn, requires X at his young age to be
picked up and dropped off in the parking lot of a nearby supermarket rather
in front of Madame’s residence. In short, the issue makes it more difficult for
X to be picked up and dropped off. The filming of the exchange of X at every
pick up and drop off does not help the situation either.

[116]

Unless stopped, the lack of cooperation
between the parties and their mistrust of one another will continue to have a
direct impact on X. These two issues will also no doubt affect X’s best
interests going forward. While as adults, X’s parents made certain decisions
that did not work out for them, they must now focus on making sound decisions
that work best for X.

[117]

Going forward, in the best interests of X,
Monsieur and Madame must find ways or seek help in order to find ways to
cooperate with one another concerning his well-being and physical and
emotional needs. In order for the gradually increasing parenting time ordered
in this judgment to work, and for X to benefit from the presence of both his
mother and father in his life, his parents must focus on the best interests
of X who will remain their son for the years to come.

[118]

The child hand buckle fracture issue is a good
example. Children are meant to play and playing comes with risks, especially
for some maybe more than others depending on their personalities and physical
capabilities. If a child has an accident, big or small, during the time that
he or she is with her mother or father, both parents must let the other know
so that the child’s safety is not in any way compromised. This is not
something that is optional. It is a must. Both parents must exercise enough
introspection and care to ensure by effective communication that their child
comes first.

[119]

This brings me to a final issue, which is that
of child support. Before me, Madame indicated that she is not seeking child
support for X because she is financially in a position not to need one. While
no doubt a fact, this is not the issue. Child support is of public order and
it must be ordered for the benefit of the child.

[120]

In this case, however, seeing that this matter
is being transferred to the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, the current
income of Monsieur, which I understand to be about $30,000 and the facts that
he is going to be incurring costs to secure a dwelling in Ontario and going
back and forth between City A and City B in order to spend more time with X,
I will not order such support leaving the issue for the Ontario Superior
Court of Justice to address, if and when appropriate.

Article 3

The removal or the retention of a child is to be considered wrongful
where –

(a)

it is in breach of
custody attributed to a person, an institution or any other body, either
jointly or alone, under the law of the State in which the child was habitually
resident immediately before the removal or retention; and

(b)

at the time of removal
or retention those rights were actually exercised, either jointly or alone, or
would have been so exercised but for the removal or retention.
